newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: S&P sees tough environment for NZ insurers.
newsitem.headline: S&P sees tough environment for NZ insurers.

text.p: Standard and Poor's said on Thursday New Zealand's general insurance industry would continue to operate in a difficult environment in the short term.

"The New Zealand general insurance industry's operating environment will continue to be difficult in the near term, reflecting the highly competitive nature of the industry coupled with inadequate pricing and adverse claims experience in some lines," S&P said in a paper prepared for an insurance briefing.

While underwriting losses had largely centred in the personal lines of private motor and household in 1996, lower reinsurance rates and some cross subsidisation from earthquake classes had led to a softening in commercial lines.
As a consequence, the net combined operating ratio was expected to deteriorate to about 100-102 percent in 1996/7 from 96.9 percent in 1995.
Despite competitive pressures, insurers had taken strong action in personal lines of insurance by raising premium rates.
"As a consequence, S&P believes the industry is approaching the bottom of the underwriting cycle," S&P said.
The New Zealand insurance market as a whole carried a relatively high median rating of A plus, reflecting high foreign ownership and well-structured participants.
However, associated with the withdrawal of the Earthquake Commission from the commercial earthquake market, the private sector was assuming a greater level of aggregate risk.
"This, combined with the apparent cross subsidisation of some commercial lines and a softening of premium rates, makes for a high risk cocktail which may haunt the industry."

S&P said approporate reinsurance protection and establishment of contingency reserves would assist balance sheets, but only adequate pricing of risk would allow the industry to maintain its strength over the long term.
The broad outlook for pricing was a continuation of upward adjustments in domestic lines and further weakening in the pricing of commercial lines.

S&P said insurers started repricing in response to claims experience in some personal and small commercial lines, mainly due to increasing crime trends, especially in the Auckland area, and vehicle claims costs, late last year.
Despite this action, the lagged nature of the earnings would mean it would be 12 months before the benefit of these moves flowed through to the industry's profit and loss account.

S&P said the levels of premium discounting seen in this year were not sustainable and that it expected some positive adjustment in 1997, though the underlying conditions driving the discounting would remain.
This scenario assumed the continuing excess capacity in global reinssurance and the absence of a major event.
New entrants would continue to fuel highly competitive conditions and provide excess capacity generally,
S&P said the ratings outlook for most New Zealand general insurers was stable, based mainly on ownership factors and the expected return to industry profitability in the medium term.

"S&P anticipates the industry's return to profitability in the next two to three years. The current cycle is considered to be approaching the bottom, and for the most part reported results are within the tolerances of ratings assigned," it said.
